content.p: On Monday 29 September 1941, tens of thousands of Jewish residents of Kyiv, carrying documents and warm clothes, walked toward the city's cemeteries in the belief that they were being resettled. Most of them never left the ravine behind the cemetery. Over the next day and a half, German SS and police units, helped by local auxiliaries, shot them in small groups. Sonderkommando 4a reported that it and its partners had killed 33,771 Jews in two days. Historians have described the shootings at Babi Yar as one of the largest single massacres of the Second World War.

The ravine remained a killing ground until the autumn of 1943. The Germans then tried to erase the evidence, and the Soviet state later tried to bury the memory of what had happened there, so for decades the site was as much a fight over remembrance as a crime scene.

German forces entered Kyiv on 19 September 1941, and the city became part of the Reichskommissariat Ukraine under Erich Koch. The US Holocaust Memorial Museum says about 160,000 Jews had lived there before the invasion, around a fifth of the population. About 100,000 of them fled or were serving in the Soviet military, which left roughly 60,000 in the city, mostly women, children, the elderly and the ill.

In the first week of the occupation two large explosions destroyed the German headquarters and part of the main street, Khreshchatyk, and killed a number of German soldiers and officials. The museum states that the blasts came from mines left by retreating Soviet forces, and that the Germans used the sabotage as a pretext to murder the Jews who remained. The Kyiv Post reported that the first German reaction, after the explosions of 24 September, was to arrest 1,600 Jews.

The Kyiv Post places a meeting of senior officers on 26 September: the SS and police leader Friedrich Jeckeln, Einsatzgruppe C's commander Otto Rasch, Blobel, and the army's commandant of Kyiv, Major General Kurt Eberhard. It says they planned a "gross Aktion" against about 50,000 Jews, and that a radio report to Berlin said the army command was "very satisfied" with the measures. The German agency bpb dates the meeting to 27 September and says members of the Wehrmacht attended. It adds that two police battalions, numbered 45 and 303, were already used for a "cleansing" and cordon duty at Babi Yar on that day, and that a few dozen Sinti and Roma had been shot there on 23 September. It says the number of victims in those first shootings can no longer be established.

According to the Kyiv Post, an army propaganda company printed 2,000 posters in three languages on 27 September. They ordered the Jews of Kyiv and its suburbs to appear at the junction of two streets near the cemeteries at 8 a.m. on 29 September, with documents, money, valuables and warm clothing. "Those Jews who do not carry out this order and are found in another place will be shot," the notice added. The wording suggested a relocation. The Kyiv Post says former Soviet militiamen recruited by the SS spread a rumour that the Jews would be taken to a port and shipped to Palestine, and that the confusing location on the poster made a train deportation sound believable. Raisa Maistrenko, who was three at the time, later recalled that her family did not think they were walking to their deaths: "We thought they would transport us to Palestine."

The Kyiv Post describes Babi Yar as a ravine about 2.5 kilometres long and 50 metres deep, chosen for its size and remoteness. It reports that about 50 officers of Sonderkommando 4a under Blobel supervised some 1,200 German policemen and a few hundred Ukrainian auxiliaries. Historian Jeffrey Veidlinger writes that the crowd, mostly women, children and the elderly because the Soviet government had already mobilised the men fit to fight, was marched under guard through a barbed-wire enclosure.

The people were robbed of money, possessions and documents, forced to undress, and led into the ravine, where they were shot, according to the USHMM and the bpb. The bpb says Wehrmacht soldiers helped cordon off the area and that victims were made to lie face down before being shot in the back of the neck, with the pile of bodies covered at intervals with sand. Veidlinger puts the killing at some 36 hours. He and the Kyiv Post disagree on one point about the auxiliaries: Veidlinger writes that Ukrainian prisoners recruited as local police took part, while the Kyiv Post says only German police and SS men did the shooting and that the identity of the Ukrainian-speaking police who herded the victims remains unknown. It adds that no document places either of the two Ukrainian nationalist formations suspected of involvement at Babi Yar.

The survivor Dina Pronicheva, an actress who held a Soviet passport recording her as Russian, described her experience in a written testimony held by Yad Vashem. Her Jewish mother urged her to leave, but she would not abandon her. A policeman told a German officer not to believe her claim to be Russian, and she was sent to the edge of the pit. She fell before the shots, lay among the dead through the night, and escaped in the dark. An 11-year-old boy named Fima Shnaiderman followed her out and was killed by a shot as they climbed. Girl Museum notes that only 29 people are known to have survived the massacre.

The figure of 33,771 comes from the perpetrators. A report relayed from Heydrich's office on 2 October 1941 said that Sonderkommando 4a, with the Einsatzgruppe staff and two police commandos, had shot that number on 29 and 30 September, according to the Kyiv Post. The German 6th Army's intelligence report quoted by the same paper said about 34,000 had reported and that all had been killed. Veidlinger's article gives the German figure as 33,371, which looks like a transposition, since every other page gives 33,771. The bpb notes that the Nuremberg tribunal relied on the unit's own report, that not every victim was probably registered, and that many victims remain unnamed. Yad Vashem, as the bpb cites it, puts the figure at more than 33,000 Jews.

The figure for the whole occupation is less certain still. The USHMM says Soviet investigations in 1943 concluded that about 100,000 people were murdered at Babi Yar. The bpb gives an estimate of about 65,000 and says the Soviet state commission of 1944 thought the number could exceed 100,000. Veidlinger counts another 70,000 after the September massacre, and Girl Museum says nearly 100,000 were buried there. Among those killed in the later period were Roma, patients of a psychiatric hospital, Soviet prisoners of war and non-Jewish civilians.

The Kyiv Post says the SS shipped more than 100 trucks of clothing and valuables taken from the victims, some for ethnic Germans and some for 25,000 people who had lost their homes in the explosions, and that the Jews' apartments were redistributed.

As the Red Army drew closer, the Germans tried to remove the evidence. The Holocaust Historical Society says Reinhard Heydrich ordered Blobel in May 1942 to take charge of destroying mass graves, the operation known as Sonderaktion 1005, and that Blobel was back at Babi Yar in June 1943 to show the work crew where to dig. The USHMM says the Syrets labour education camp, set up beside the ravine in May 1942, supplied about 300 prisoners for the task. The Kyiv Post gives 330. Emory University's Holocaust Denial on Trial project says they worked chained by the feet from August to September 1943, burning bodies on pyres built on rails, with tombstones from the nearby Jewish cemetery used as the base. Survivor David Budnik remembered 60 furnaces, each burning more than 2,000 corpses. The project says each pyre held 2,500 to 3,000 bodies.

The workers expected to be killed when the job was over. According to the project, they escaped together on 29 September 1943, and several survived to give accounts. The USHMM confirms that most of the cover-up prisoners were murdered, but that a handful escaped and later testified to the Soviets. The Kyiv Post says the task was so large that it probably was not finished. The USHMM adds that the killings at the ravine stopped only days before the Soviets retook Kyiv on 6 November 1943.

A Soviet court in Kyiv put 15 German policemen on trial in January 1946 over Babi Yar; Pronicheva gave evidence. In 1947 Blobel was one of 24 defendants in the American military tribunal's Einsatzgruppen trial at Nuremberg. He pleaded not guilty, his defence said he had followed orders, and he was convicted and sentenced to death. He was hanged at Landsberg on 8 June 1951.

The Reichskommissar, Erich Koch, was tried by a Polish court in 1959 and sentenced to death for crimes in occupied Poland, but the USHMM says he was never tried for his crimes in Ukraine. His sentence was commuted to life because of ill health, and he died in prison in 1986.

In 1968, the Jewish Telegraphic Agency reported, seven former SS men from a wartime commando unit began prison terms of four to 15 years after a 14-month trial that covered 200 mass-murder cases, Babi Yar the best known. Three other defendants were not sentenced because, the agency reported, they were found not guilty under 1941 military law. The longest sentence, 15 years, went to Kuno Kalsen, then 56, though prosecutors had asked for life.
content.h2: Silence, a dam and a poem
content.p: The Soviet authorities did not publicise what had happened. The Kyiv Post says an early call for a memorial, made soon after the Red Army returned, was crushed by Nikita Khrushchev, who led the party in Ukraine. It reports that in 1957 his successor, Mykola Podhorny, ordered the ravine filled in. Engineers built a dam instead and pumped brickworks waste behind it. On 13 March 1961 the dam burst and a wall of mud swept over homes, a tram depot and a stadium. The Kyiv Post estimates 24 deaths; Veidlinger says at least 145 people died.

Viktor Nekrasov wrote in 1959 that there was no monument at Babi Yar, and the poet Yevgeny Yevtushenko's poem on the ravine followed in 1961. Shostakovich dedicated his 13th Symphony to Babi Yar in 1962, and the writer Anatolii Kuznetsov published a censored novel-document on the massacre in 1966, which appeared uncensored in 1970 after he defected to Britain. Meanwhile, according to the Kyiv Post, work began in 1962 on a television headquarters on the site of the Jewish cemetery, where graves were dug up and headstones destroyed.

On 29 September 1966 an unauthorised gathering at the ravine heard speeches from Pronicheva, Nekrasov and the dissident writer Ivan Dzyuba, the Kyiv Post reports. Afterwards the authorities put up a small granite stone promising a monument. The first official monument arrived in 1976 and commemorated "Soviet citizens and POWs"; Veidlinger writes that it said nothing about Jews, and the Kyiv Post that it stood blocks from the ravine. Veidlinger explains the omission as part of a Soviet wartime story that played down the specifically racial aim of Nazi policy, and avoided questions about collaboration.

A menorah-shaped monument to the Jewish victims was unveiled after Ukraine's independence. The USHMM and Veidlinger date it to 29 September 1991, the 50th anniversary, while the Kyiv Post says Jewish organisations put it up in 1992. The site is now a public park, where, the USHMM notes, monuments to many different groups of victims have been added. Veidlinger observes that this has made the site as contested as the war itself.

A commission to build a larger memorial was formed only in 2016, according to Veidlinger. The planned Babi Yar Holocaust Memorial Center, with a virtual-reality museum conceived by the artistic director Ilya Khrzhanovsky, has drawn wide controversy, and one critic dismissed it as a "Holocaust Disneyland".

On 1 March 2022, during Russia's invasion, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a Russian strike on a Kyiv TV tower killed five people and damaged the nearby memorial site. "What is the point of saying 'never again' for 80 years," he asked, "if the world stays silent when a bomb drops on the same site of Babyn Yar?"
